title: Live Resin vs. Live Rosin: Differences, Pros and Prices
h1: Live Resin or Live Rosin? How They're Made and Which to Choose
metaDescription: Live resin vs. live rosin, side by side: what "live" means, solvent vs. solventless extraction, terpenes, flavor, potency, price and how to choose.
excerpt: Both start with fresh-frozen cannabis. One is extracted with a solvent, the other with ice water and a heat press. Here's how they compare and how to pick.
keyTakeaways: "Live" means the plants were frozen right after harvest instead of dried and cured, to keep more of their terpenes.
Live resin is extracted with a hydrocarbon solvent that is purged afterward; live rosin uses only ice water, heat and pressure.
Rosin is often priced higher, since separating resin without solvents yields less oil and takes more hands-on work.
Both are strong concentrates, so start with a very small amount and check the THC figure on the label.
body:
Live resin vs. live rosin comes down to how the oil leaves the plant. Both begin with cannabis that was frozen the moment it was harvested. Live resin is then extracted with a solvent, while live rosin is pressed from ice-water hash using nothing but heat and pressure. That one step shapes the texture, the price and, for many people, the flavor.

## Why terpenes are the point of "live" concentrates

Terpenes are the aromatic compounds behind every strain's smell, from lemon peel to pine to fuel. Researchers credit terpenes, not cannabinoids, with the aroma of cannabis, and both are made in the plant's tiny resin glands, called trichomes. Our guide to [cannabis terpenes](/blog/what-are-cannabis-terpenes/) covers them in depth.

Many terpenes are volatile. The lighter ones fade as cannabis dries and sits in storage, so cured flower rarely smells as loud as a living plant. Live concentrates are built to catch more of that fresh aroma.

## What "live" means: fresh-frozen cannabis

Most flower is dried for a week or two, then cured before it's packaged. Live products skip that stage: the plants are frozen fresh, without drying, and kept frozen until extraction day.

Cold storage slows the loss of volatile compounds such as terpenes, and the cold also makes the resin glands brittle, which matters to rosin makers. The trade calls this starting material fresh frozen, and both products begin there.

## How live resin is made

Live resin is a solvent extract. At a licensed processor, technicians wash the frozen plant material with a chilled hydrocarbon solvent, usually butane or propane, inside closed equipment. The solvent dissolves the cannabinoids and aroma compounds and leaves most of the plant matter behind.

Next comes the purge, which removes the solvent under mild conditions. Then the extract is worked into its final form: controlled heating and crystallization can separate THCA crystals, called diamonds, from a terpene-rich sauce, and other batches become sugar or badder. Our overview of [cannabis extraction methods](/blog/types-of-cannabis-extraction/) explains how these techniques compare.

Hydrocarbon extraction has become the dominant way to make non-distilled concentrates for dabbing and vaping. Licensed live resin sold in Michigan has also passed state-required lab testing before it reaches a dispensary shelf.

## How live rosin is made

Live rosin is solventless. Nothing goes into the process except water, ice, heat and pressure, and it happens in two stages.

1. **Wash.** The frozen plants are stirred gently in ice water. The cold makes the resin glands brittle, so they break away and can be separated from the softer plant material. What's collected is ice-water hash, which has to be dried before it's pressed.
2. **Press.** The dried hash is pressed between heated plates, and the heat and pressure squeeze out the oil. Some makers then let it rest in cool storage, which changes its texture to a badder or jam.

For the full process, read our [solventless live rosin explainer](/blog/solventless-live-rosin-101/).

## Live resin vs. live rosin: key differences

| | Live resin | Live rosin |
|---|---|---|
| Starting material | Fresh-frozen flower | Fresh-frozen flower, washed into ice-water hash |
| How it's extracted | Hydrocarbon solvent, then purged | Ice water, then heat and pressure |
| Common textures | Sauce, sugar, badder, diamonds | Badder, jam, sauce-like rosin |
| Flavor | Bright and terpene-forward | Terpene-forward; fans say it tastes closest to the plant |
| Yield per batch | Higher | Lower |
| Price | Varies by product | Often priced higher |

Flavor is personal. Some people taste little difference, while others prefer rosin's clean, hash-like finish. Potency overlaps too: both are concentrates, so compare the THC figures on the labels instead of assuming one is stronger.

Price is the clearest gap. Separating resin without solvents yields less oil and takes more hands-on work, so rosin is often priced higher. For today's prices, check your store's live menu.

## What they have in common

- Both start with fresh-frozen cannabis rather than dried and cured flower.
- Both aim to keep as much of the plant's terpene profile as possible.
- Both are potent, so a serving is tiny compared with flower.
- Both can be dabbed, and both turn up in vape cartridges.
- Licensed versions of both pass Michigan's required testing before they're sold.

They sit alongside shatter, wax, kief and the rest of the family covered in our [guide to cannabis concentrates](/blog/marijuana-concentrates/).

## Carts or dabs? Formats for each

**Dabs.** Both come in small jars for a dab rig, an electronic rig or a dab pen. A lower temperature keeps more of the flavor, since heat speeds the loss of terpenes. Start with the smallest portion you can manage, or add a little to a bowl of flower instead.

**Vape carts.** Live resin is widely used in vape cartridges. Live rosin carts and pods exist too, so check what your store carries. When shoppers weigh live rosin vs. live resin carts, price and availability often decide it.

**Other uses.** See our look at [how people use live resin](/blog/live-resin-benefits-uses/) for more ways to enjoy it.

## Which one should you choose?

Choose live resin if you want rich flavor, often at a friendlier price, or if you mostly use vape carts. Choose live rosin if you'd rather have a product made without solvents and don't mind paying more. If you're new to concentrates, either one is a big step up from flower, so take a small amount and wait before having more.

At High Society, concentrates and vape pens are both on the menu, and what's in stock varies by store. [Browse your store's menu](/shop/), order ahead for in-store or curbside pickup, and ask our budtenders to compare the textures with you. Shopping is for adults 21 and older, or 18 and older with a valid medical marijuana card.

faq.q: Is live rosin better than live resin?
faq.a: Not across the board. Rosin is solventless, and many enthusiasts prize its flavor. Live resin also carries a rich terpene profile, often at a lower price, and it's widely used in vape carts. The better pick depends on your budget, how you like to consume and whether a solventless process matters to you.

faq.q: Why is live rosin so expensive?
faq.a: Mostly yield and labor. Separating resin glands with ice water instead of a solvent tends to yield less, and pressing that hash returns only part of its weight as oil. The process is also hands-on, so rosin is often priced higher than solvent extracts. Check your store's live menu for current prices.

No. Live resin is made with a solvent, usually a hydrocarbon such as butane or propane, which is purged out before the product is finished. Licensed products sold in Michigan pass state-required lab testing, and the label names the lab and the test date. If you want a concentrate made without solvents, look for rosin instead.

Buy them only from a licensed dispensary. Licensed carts in Michigan are lab tested, while the 2019 vaping lung-injury outbreak was tied mainly to THC vapes from informal sources and to vitamin E acetate. Any inhaled product carries some risk, so go easy, never modify a cart, and talk to your doctor if you have heart or lung concerns.

claims.claim: Terpenes, not cannabinoids, give cannabis its aroma; both are made in the resin glands (trichomes)
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3165946/ ("Terpenoids, not cannabinoids, are responsible for the aroma of cannabis"; "synthesized in cannabis, in secretory cells inside glandular trichomes")

claims.claim: Lighter terpenes fade as cannabis dries and sits in storage
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3165946/ (monoterpenes "do suffer diminished yields with drying and storage")

claims.claim: Most flower is hung to dry for days, then cured for weeks before it's trimmed and packaged
claims.fix: Rewritten: dried for a week or two, then cured before packaging. Trimming comes before or after drying, never after curing; no curing duration is stated
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11821007/ (Cornell, 2025: "drying usually take 1–2 weeks"; plants dried "by hanging the whole plant upside down on strings, or wet-trimming then drying the inflorescence on trays")

claims.claim: Growers freeze the plants within hours of cutting, often whole
claims.fix: Timing and 'often whole' removed; now: the plants are frozen fresh, without drying, and kept frozen until extraction
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13382692/ ("Fresh-frozen cannabis inflorescence ... stored at −50 °C to minimize degradation of volatile and nonvolatile constituents")

claims.claim: Freezing holds the trichomes in place, slows terpene loss and makes resin glands brittle
claims.fix: Kept only the sourced parts: cold storage slows the loss of volatiles, and cold makes the resin glands brittle
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13382692/ (frozen storage to minimize degradation of volatiles); https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12051344/ ("Ice water causes the resins to become brittle")

claims.claim: Live resin is extracted 'in a licensed lab' with butane, propane 'or a blend of the two' inside sealed equipment
claims.fix: 'Licensed lab' changed to 'licensed processor' (Michigan labs test; processors extract); unsourced blend dropped; 'closed equipment'
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13382692/ ("Frozen biomass is typically contacted with chilled liquid hydrocarbons such as n-butane"; solvents "such as n-butane, iso-butane, or propane"; vacuum applied to the extraction system)

claims.claim: The purge uses gentle heat and vacuum; the extract becomes sauce, sugar, badder or diamonds
claims.fix: Now: the solvent is removed under mild conditions, and controlled heating and crystallization can separate THCA crystals (diamonds) from a terpene-rich sauce
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13382692/ ("the solvent removed under mild conditions"; "controlled heating and crystallization, are often used to separate THCA-rich fractions from the remaining liquid high terpene extract")

claims.claim: Solvent extraction is efficient, so it pulls a lot of oil from each batch
claims.fix: Replaced with the sourced point that hydrocarbon extraction is the dominant method for non-distilled concentrates for dabbing and vaping
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13382692/ (hydrocarbon extraction "has become the dominant method for producing inhalable-grade non-distilled concentrates")

claims.claim: Licensed live resin and rosin sold in Michigan have passed state-required lab testing; the label names the lab and test date
claims.source: law-facts mi-labeling (R 420.504(1): testing lab and test date on every label); hs-facts compliance.testing ("products that have passed Michigan's stringent testing standards")

claims.claim: Live rosin is solventless: ice water, heat and pressure
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12183170/ ("'rosin' refers to a solventless extract obtained through mechanical compression (heat and pressure)")

claims.claim: Ice-water wash: brittle heads snap off, are caught in mesh bags and freeze-dried; hash pressed in filter bags into a golden oil, then rested a few days into badder or jam
claims.fix: Kept what the sources support (cold makes glands brittle and separable, the hash must be dried, heat and pressure release the oil); mesh-bag, freeze-dryer, filter-bag and 'few days' details dropped; cool rest kept as 'some makers'
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12051344/ ("wet fractionation through mechanical agitation of plant flowers in ice water"; "the need for subsequent dewatering"); https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12183170/

claims.claim: Rosin usually costs more because each batch yields less oil and takes more skilled labor
claims.fix: Softened to 'often priced higher', with the yield reason tied to the source; no price figures (brief: prices only from the live menu)
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12051344/ (mechanical trichome separation: "To get the high-purity product, a cold, dry atmosphere and a short processing time are required. However, under these conditions, the yield is low."); no independent price data found

claims.claim: Potency overlaps, so compare the THC figures on the labels
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13422286/ (legal Ontario products: "live resin from 58% to 87%", "rosin ranging from 0% to 86%" THC)

claims.claim: Most people dab live rosin; live resin carts are easy to find because the oil flows well; rosin carts are less common and cost more
claims.fix: Usage and flow claims removed; now: live resin is widely used in carts, rosin carts and pods exist, check your store
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13382692/ (hydrocarbon extracts dominate inhalable non-distilled concentrates); no source found for usage shares or flow

claims.claim: A portion about the size of a grain of rice is a common place to start
claims.fix: Replaced with 'start with the smallest portion you can manage': no source gives a portion size, and a rice-grain dab of a 60-70% THC concentrate is a large dose
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9036911/ (concentrates average "60.3% ... to 68.7%" THC); https://nida.nih.gov/research-topics/cannabis-marijuana ("Dabbing can rapidly deliver large amounts of THC to the body")

claims.claim: A lower temperature keeps more of the flavor
claims.fix: Added the reason (heat speeds terpene loss)
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12251074/ ("elevated temperatures accelerate the volatilization and degradation of terpenes")

claims.claim: Some makers use live resin or rosin in gummies or infused pre-rolls
claims.fix: Removed; the paragraph now only links the sibling article

claims.claim: The 2019 lung-injury outbreak was tied mainly to THC vapes from informal sources and to vitamin E acetate
claims.source: https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/tobacco/basic_information/e-cigarettes/severe-lung-disease.html ("Vitamin E acetate is strongly linked to the EVALI outbreak"; THC products "particularly from informal sources like friends, family, or in-person or online dealers, are linked to most EVALI cases")

claims.claim: High Society: concentrates and vape pens on the menu, order ahead for in-store or curbside pickup, budtenders help you choose, 21+ or 18+ with a medical card

review.notes: Fact-check 2026-10-24 (fact-check): 19 claims checked, 11 fixed (1 wrong, 6 unsupported, 4 overstated). Sources added: Sosa 2026, MacGowan 2025, Munger 2025. Every listed source was opened this session except the CRA rules PDF, which is used as law-facts lists it (michigan.gov refuses automated fetches). No prices; no residual-solvent claim (not in law-facts).
